problems.title: Counting sectors
problems.statement: A warp loads 4-byte floats; lane ℓ reads element $o + s\ell$ of an array that starts on a 128-byte boundary.
problems.solution: (a) bytes 0–127: 4 sectors. (b) bytes 4–131: 5. (c) bytes 0–255, every sector touched: 8, (d) 50%.

problems.title: Element size and instruction count
problems.statement: Read 1 MiB contiguously with fully coalesced warp loads.
hints: A warp moves 32 × element size bytes per instruction.
problems.solution: (a) 32,768, (b) 8,192, (c) 2,048. All are 100% sector-efficient; the difference is instructions issued. Narrow loads can make a memory-bound kernel issue-bound.

problems.title: Stride 3
problems.solution: Addresses span bytes 0–375; consecutive lanes are 12 bytes apart, less than a sector, so every sector in the span is touched: 12 sectors, efficiency $128/384 = 33.3\%$. In general, stride $s \le 8$ costs $4s$ sectors.

problems.title: Misaligned float4
problems.statement: Each lane loads 16 bytes; lane ℓ starts at byte $16\ell + 4$ (the buffer is offset by one float).
problems.solution: Span 4–515 covers sectors 0 through 16: 17 sectors for 512 bytes, $94.1\%$. (On real hardware a misaligned float4 load isn't even legal: vector loads must be naturally aligned. Alignment matters more for vector loads than for scalar ones.)

problems.title: Gathering from a small table
problems.statement: Each lane loads a float at a uniformly random index into a table, independently.

parts.prompt: Table of 1 GiB: expected sectors per warp load (to the nearest integer)?
Table of 4 KiB (128 sectors): expected distinct sectors?

hints: Expected distinct values among 32 draws from m: $m(1 - (1 - 1/m)^{32})$.
problems.solution: (a) Collisions are negligible: 32 sectors, 12.5% efficiency. (b) $128(1 - (127/128)^{32}) = 28.4$: barely better. Small tables help through caching (they stay in L1/L2), not through coalescing.

problems.title: Two half-rows
problems.statement: A 16 × 16 block reads a row-major float image; warp 0 covers x = 0–15 of rows 0 and 1. The image starts on a 128-byte boundary.
problems.solution: (a) Each half-row is 64 bytes, starting at 0 and 4096: 2 sectors each, 4 in all. (b) Row 1 starts at byte 4004, which is 4 bytes past a sector boundary, so its 64 bytes straddle 3 sectors: 5 in all. Row pitch alignment matters whenever a warp spans rows.

problems.title: Partial-sector writes
problems.statement: A warp stores floats at stride 2. Suppose the memory system must read each partially written sector, merge, and write it back.
problems.solution: 8 sectors, each needing a 32-byte read and a 32-byte write: 512 bytes for 128 useful, 4×. Scattered or strided stores can cost more than the same loads; making them full-sector is worth extra effort.

problems.title: What coalescing costs at scale
problems.statement: A memory-bound kernel moves 1 GB between L2 and the SMs per run (simulator: bytesMoved), with coalescing 25%.

parts.prompt: Time at full 512 GB/s, in ms?
Time if fully coalesced, in ms?

problems.solution: (a) 1.953 ms, (b) 0.488 ms, (c) 4×. A memory-bound kernel's runtime is proportional to sectors moved.

problems.title: DRAM's physical reality
problems.statement: DRAM reads activate a whole row into a row buffer, then stream bursts from it.

parts.prompt: Which costs the least per useful byte?
Nsight Compute reports 16 sectors per request for a kernel's 4-byte loads. The simplest pattern that explains it is…

hints: Activations are expensive; bursts are cheap.
problems.solution: (a) Consecutive bytes in one open row: one activation, one burst. (b) $4s = 16 \Rightarrow s = 4$, 25% efficiency, for example a 16-byte struct read one field at a time.

problems.title: Same bytes, any order
problems.statement: Lane ℓ reads float $\pi(\ell)$ where π is a permutation of 0–31.

parts.prompt: On modern NVIDIA GPUs, is this slower than lane ℓ reading float ℓ?
options: No: the same sectors are fetched once each

hints: Sectors depend on the set of addresses, not their order.
problems.solution: The set of addresses is the same 128 bytes, so 4 sectors. Early CUDA GPUs required lanes in order; modern ones just count distinct sectors.
